t: Number of Students Doing Homework at a Given Time — Editorial
o: Each student i is 'busy' during the inclusive interval [startTime[i], endTime[i]]. We simply need to count how many of these intervals contain queryTime. In Example 1, intervals are [1,3], [2,2], [3,7]; only [3,7] contains 4, so the answer is 1. In Example 2, the single interval [4,4] contains 4 (endpoints count), so the answer is 1. With n ≤ 100 and values ≤ 1000, even an O(n) scan or a counting array over times is trivially fast — no clever data structures needed.
k: A student is busy at queryTime iff startTime[i] <= queryTime <= endTime[i]; just test this condition per student.
Intervals are inclusive on both ends, so a zero-length interval like [4,4] still counts when queryTime = 4.
With n ≤ 100, a single linear pass is optimal; any fancier structure is unnecessary.

a.i: Check every student's interval directly against queryTime and count matches. Since each check is O(1) and there are n students, this is already optimal for this problem size.
s: For each index i from 0 to n-1, test whether startTime[i] <= queryTime <= endTime[i].
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter is used.

a.i: Treat each interval as +1 at its start and -1 at its end+1, then sweep over time accumulating a running sum; the value at queryTime equals the number of active intervals. This generalizes to many queries after O(n + maxT) preprocessing.
s: Create an array diff of size max(endTime) + 2, initialized to 0.
For each student, do diff[startTime[i]] += 1 and diff[endTime[i] + 1] -= 1.
Sweep t from 1 upward, maintaining running = running + diff[t].
When t == queryTime, return the current running sum.
a.t: O(n + T) where T = max(endTime); building the difference array is O(n), the sweep is O(T).

w: In an interview, lead with the linear scan — it's one line of logic, provably optimal here since every interval must be examined in the worst case. Mention the difference-array approach as a follow-up answer if asked to handle many queries efficiently: preprocess once in O(n + T), then answer each query in O(1). Common pitfalls: forgetting that intervals are inclusive (so [4,4] counts at time 4), and off-by-one errors when decrementing at endTime + 1 in the sweep version. Edge cases: single-student input, zero-length intervals, and queryTime equal to a start or end boundary. A likely follow-up: 'What if there are millions of queries?' — answer with the difference array plus prefix sums, or sort events and binary search if times were unbounded.
